newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bond futures off to a flying start.
newsitem.headline: Australian bond futures off to a flying start.

text.p: *Australian bond futures got off to a flying start as a technically inspired rally caught the market short and saw a strong outperformance against U.S. Treasuries.
*U.S. CPI for March due later on Tuesday.
Australian bond futures got off to a flying start as a technically-inspired rally caught the market short and saw a strong outperformance against U.S. Treasuries, traders said.

"What you are seeing is the market repricing itself against the U.S.," said one trader. "People thought we had gone too far when (the spread) got to 120-130 over, and in the past week that has been reversed, particularly in the light of the jobs data."
The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread slipped to around 94 basis points in the initial flurry, in lowest level since mid-February.
The early rally also saw resistance at 92.010 on the June 10-year bond futures contract, although the market failed to sustain a move through 92.050.
"Most of the early move has been in futures. We haven't seen anything through our physical desk," added one traded.

The 10-year contract touched a high of 92.080 last week after a weak Australian labour force report, but the market was subsequently knocked back in after hours trading on Friday as U.S. Treasuries tumbled on a jump in core PPI inflation and upward revisions to retail sales data earlier this year.
The U.S. market faces the March CPI later on Tuesday.
The current U.S. data flow is suggesting that the Federal Reserve will tighten policy again when the Federal Open Market Committee meets in May, analysts said.

The Reserve Bank is not seen following the U.S. move, and there has even been speculation in recent days that the central bank may ease again after the jobs report and as long as the upcoming quarterly CPI and average weekly earnings reports, and the verdict on the "living wage" claim, all prove benign.
Indeed, the June bank bills futures contract has rallied to be back in line with the current 6.0 percent cash rate, having been discounting a 25 basis point tightening in early March.

The early move also saw the local market outperform Canadian debt, which had also shown some resistance to the minor fall in U.S. prices on Monday. However, N.Z. bonds outshone the bloc following a much weaker than expected set of inflation data for the March quarter.
